chapterNote: The empire's machinery for replacing a queen becomes, unknowingly, the means of setting a Jewish orphan on the throne. Two hidden things run beneath the chapter: Esther's concealed identity, kept on Mordecai's charge, and Mordecai's quiet loyalty in foiling an assassination — a good deed left unrewarded and written into the royal record, where it will wait for exactly the right night.

1.text: After these things, when the rage of King Ahasuerus had cooled, he remembered Vashti — what she had done, and what had been decreed against her.

2.text: Then the king's attendants who served him said, "Let a search be made for the king for beautiful young virgins.

3.text: Let the king appoint commissioners in every province of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in the fortress of Susa, into the care of Hegai the king's eunuch, keeper of the women, and let their beauty-treatments be given them.

4.text: Then let the young woman who most pleases the king become queen in place of Vashti." The plan pleased the king, and he did so.

5.text: Now in the fortress of Susa there was a Jew named Mordecai son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite,

6.text: who had been carried into exile from Jerusalem among the captives taken with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had led away.
6.notes: Mordecai's pedigree roots him in the covenant people carried to Babylon a century before. He is a son of the exile — a Jew making a life in a foreign empire, exactly the situation the book is written to speak into.

7.text: He had brought up Hadassah — that is, Esther — his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was shapely and beautiful, and when her father and mother died, Mordecai had taken her as his own daughter.
7.amp: he was rearing Hadassah [hadassah (H1919) — myrtle], that is, Esther [likely from Persian stara, 'star'], his cousin, for she had no father or mother.
7.notes: Two names for one girl: Hadassah, 'myrtle,' the Hebrew name of her people; Esther, her Persian court-name. The double name is the whole plot in miniature — a covenant identity hidden inside a Gentile one.

8.text: So when the king's order and decree were heard, and many young women were gathered to the fortress of Susa under Hegai's care, Esther too was taken to the king's palace, into the care of Hegai, keeper of the women.

9.text: The young woman pleased him and won his favor, so he quickly gave her the beauty-treatments and her allotted food, and assigned to her seven chosen maids from the king's palace, and moved her and her maids to the best place in the harem.
9.notes: Esther 'wins favor' at every stage — with Hegai here, with the king in v.17, with all who see her. The narrator never says God grants it, but the steady, unforced favor falling on this hidden Jewess is the book's fingerprint of providence.

10.text: Esther had not made known her people or her family, for Mordecai had charged her not to tell.
10.notes: Her silence is deliberate and obedient. In a court that has just legislated wifely submission, and where being a foreigner will soon be a capital charge, concealment is survival — and it positions her, unrecognized, precisely where she must be.

11.text: Every day Mordecai would walk back and forth in front of the courtyard of the harem, to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.

12.text: Now each young woman's turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after she had completed twelve months under the rules for the women — for so the days of their beautifying were filled: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with perfumes and cosmetics for women.

13.text: And when the young woman went in to the king in this way, she was given whatever she asked to take with her from the harem into the palace.

14.text: In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to a second harem, into the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch who kept the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name.

15.text: When the turn came for Esther — daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter — to go in to the king, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai the king's eunuch, keeper of the women, advised. And Esther won the admiration of all who saw her.
15.notes: Where others loaded themselves with whatever they wished (v.13), Esther takes only Hegai's counsel — an unassuming restraint that wins over 'all who saw her.' Her favor is not manufactured; it simply keeps arriving.

16.text: And so, in the seventh year of King Ahasuerus's reign, in the tenth month — the month of Tebeth — Esther was brought to him in the royal house.

17.text: And the king loved Esther more than all the other women; she won his grace and favor more than all the virgins, so he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.
17.amp: she obtained grace and favor [chen wachesed (H2580, H2617) — winsome favor and steadfast kindness] in his sight more than all the virgins, so he set the royal crown on her head.

18.text: Then the king gave a great banquet for all his officials and courtiers — the banquet of Esther — proclaimed a holiday for the provinces, and handed out gifts with royal generosity.

19.text: At the time of the second gathering of the young women, Mordecai was seated at the king's gate.

20.text: Esther had still not made known her family or her people, just as Mordecai had charged her; she went on doing what Mordecai said, as she had when he was raising her.
20.notes: Queen of Persia now, Esther still keeps her identity hidden and still heeds Mordecai — the same trust that will let him summon her to risk everything in chapter 4.

21.text: In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, two of the king's eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, keepers of the threshold, grew angry and plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.

22.text: But the plot became known to Mordecai, and he told Queen Esther, and Esther reported it to the king in Mordecai's name.

23.text: The matter was investigated and found to be so, and the two were hanged on a gallows. And it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king's presence.
23.notes: Mordecai saves the king's life and receives nothing — the debt is simply recorded and forgotten. That unpaid entry in the royal annals is a loaded gun the story leaves on the table; it goes off on a sleepless night in chapter 6.
